newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia promises aid for army, Lebed shuns meeting.
newsitem.headline: Russia promises aid for army, Lebed shuns meeting.

text.p: Russia's new Defence Council, set up in July to advise on military matters, held its first meeting on Friday, but the country's best-known military figure stayed away.
Security chief Alexander Lebed did not show up at the start of the meeting. Government spokesman Viktor Konnov said this might have been because talks started earlier than planned.
The meeting was chaired by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who is standing in while President Boris Yeltsin prepares for a open heart surgery.
Chernomyrdin said Russia needed to ensure adequate funding for the army.

Yeltsin set up the council in July as a counterbalance to the Security Council of which Lebed is the secretary. Yeltsin has been delegating more and more power to Chernomyrdin before the operation, due in the next two months.
The president insisted on Thursday that he was in charge of Russia, appearing on television and on the radio to reassure Russians about his ability to rule.
Chernomyrdin will leave Moscow for the Kazakh capital Almaty after the Defence Council meeting and will attend a summit of leaders of former Soviet states called to discuss Afghanistan.
Moscow regards the southern flank of the former Soviet Union as its strategic underbelly and Russian border guards patrol Tajikistan's 1,500-km (900-mile) frontier with Afghanistan.
Much of Afghanistan is now under the control of the Islamic Taleban militia, although Uzbek warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum holds several provinces to the north of the country.
Chernomyrdin told the Defence Council Russia's main tasks were to ensure funding and equipment for the cash-strapped Russian military and make sure soldiers were ready for action.
"It will work out a common concept for military projects... according to the constitution and other laws," he said.
Lebed, a reserve paratroop general, will leave for Brussels this weekend to attend a meeting of the Western NATO alliance.
It will be the first time the bass-voiced security chief has travelled outside Afghanistan or the former Soviet Union.
Lebed met Yeltsin for the first time in two months on Thursday and ordered his outspoken security adviser to work more amicably with Chernomyrdin and the government team.
Yeltsin said on television he had dismissed a threat by Lebed to resign over a minor matter.
"He (Lebed) needs to get down to business now, carry out the tasks he already has and make more effort to work with the premier and with the other services," Yeltsin said.
"You can't quarrel with everyone all the time. You can't settle issues that way. Our state apparatus must live in peace."

Lebed's main achievement since Yeltsin brought him into his administration between the two rounds of the Russian presidential election has been a peace deal with separatist rebels in the southern region of Chechnya.
Separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev met Chernomyrdin on Thursday and they agreed to set up a new joint body to rebuild Chechnya's war-torn economy and organise local elections there.
The State Duma lower chamber of parliament had denounced Lebed's peace deal as a capitulation to the separatists that could lead to the disintegration of the Russian Federation.
